subtopic: The pitot-static system of a large aircraft
question: In a typical airliner, how are the captain's and first officer's air data instruments supplied?

options.text: Both sets from the standby pitot and static system
Directly from pitot and static lines, with no computer
Each set by its own ADC and sources
Both sets by a single air data computer with two separate outputs

explanation: Two ADCs, each with independent pitot and static sources, feed the two sides. They can be cross-connected if one fails, which gives redundancy.

subtopic: The pitot-static system of a large aircraft
question: How are the standby altimeter and standby airspeed indicator of a typical airliner supplied?

options.text: From the first officer's air data computer through a relay
Directly from their own pitot and static sources
From both ADCs through a comparator
From the captain's air data computer

explanation: The standby instruments are pneumatic and fed by a third, separate pitot-static system. They keep working even if both ADCs or their power supplies fail.

subtopic: The pitot-static system of a large aircraft
question: How many independent pitot-static systems does a typical airliner installation have?

options.text: Three
Four, one per engine
One
Two

explanation: There is one for each ADC (captain and first officer) and one for the standby instruments. Each uses cross-coupled static vents on both sides of the fuselage.

subtopic: The pitot-static system of a large aircraft
question: Why does each of the three pitot-static systems use static vents on both sides of the fuselage?

options.text: To double the pressure fed to the ADC
To keep the systems at different temperatures
So that one vent can act as a pitot source
To reduce errors due to sideslip or yaw

explanation: Cross-coupled vents average the pressures on the two sides. In a sideslip, the higher pressure on one side and lower on the other largely cancel.

subtopic: What an air data computer does
question: What is the basic function of an air data computer?

options.text: To supply pitot pressure to the standby instruments
To turn pressures and temperature into signals
To measure the air density with a dedicated sensor
To compute the aircraft's position from measured accelerations

explanation: The ADC turns pitot pressure, static pressure and temperature into electrical outputs. These go to the displays and to many other systems.

subtopic: What an air data computer does
question: Which three inputs does an air data computer mainly use?

options.text: Static pressure, heading and attitude
Air temperature, fuel flow and the selected Mach number
Pitot pressure, ground speed and altitude
Pitot, static and air temperature

explanation: From these three it computes altitude, airspeeds, Mach number, temperature and vertical speed. Some installations add angle of attack.

subtopic: What an air data computer does
question: Which of these is NOT normally an output of an air data computer?

options.text: Mach number
Vertical speed (rate of climb)
Magnetic heading
True airspeed

explanation: Heading comes from the compass or inertial systems. The ADC outputs pressure altitude, CAS, Mach number, TAS, static and total temperature, and vertical speed.

subtopic: What an air data computer does
question: Which ADC module gives vertical speed?

options.text: A rate module fed by the altitude module
The Mach module, using the measured total air temperature
The computed airspeed module
The true airspeed module

explanation: Vertical speed is the rate of change of altitude. The rate module takes the altitude module's output and differentiates it.

subtopic: What an air data computer does
question: Which modules may an analogue ADC be internally split into?

options.text: Heading, attitude, turn and slip
Fuel, oil, temperature and pressure
Altitude, airspeed, Mach, TAS and rate
Navigation, guidance, display and flight data recording

explanation: Each module computes one quantity from the pressure and temperature inputs. Vertical speed comes from the altitude module through a rate of climb module.

subtopic: What an air data computer does
question: Why does the ADC need an air temperature input?

options.text: To compute pressure altitude
To compute TAS and static air temperature
To compute Mach number
To compute calibrated airspeed and pressure altitude

explanation: Pressure altitude, CAS and Mach number can all be found from pressures alone. TAS needs the speed of sound, which needs temperature, and so does the conversion of TAT to SAT.

subtopic: What an air data computer does
question: Which ADC outputs can be computed from pitot and static pressure alone, without any temperature input?

options.text: Altitude, CAS and Mach number
TAS, Mach and SAT
TAS and static air temperature
Altitude and TAS only

explanation: All three depend only on pressures and their ratios. TAS and SAT need the measured temperature as well.

subtopic: What an air data computer does
question: Which systems commonly receive data from an air data computer?

options.text: The magnetic compass and standby horizon
The fuel quantity and engine oil pressure gauges
The standby altimeter and standby ASI
The autopilot, FMS and transponder

explanation: The ADC is a central source of air data for many systems, including the autopilot and flight director, FMS, transponder altitude reporting, warning systems and flight recorders. The standby instruments are deliberately independent of it.

subtopic: Analogue and digital ADCs
question: What distinguishes an analogue ADC from a digital one?

options.text: It represents data by continuous quantities
It uses binary numbers sent over a digital data bus
It has no built-in test equipment
It cannot compute Mach number

explanation: Analogue computers represent measurements with continuous physical quantities such as voltage or shaft rotation. Digital ADCs convert the data into binary form for processing and transmission.

subtopic: Analogue and digital ADCs
question: In an analogue ADC's airspeed section, what turns the measured pressures into a shaft rotation?

options.text: A stepper motor controlled by a microprocessor and software
A bimetallic strip
A gyroscope and torque motor
A transducer driving a servomotor

explanation: The transducer senses the pressures and a servomotor turns a shaft. A synchro on the shaft then transmits its angle, which represents the airspeed.

subtopic: Analogue and digital ADCs
question: In an analogue ADC, what transmits the angular position of the airspeed shaft to other units?

options.text: A pitot tube
A capsule stack
A synchro
A flux valve

explanation: A CX (control transmitter) synchro produces signals that represent its shaft angle. A matching receiver elsewhere reproduces that angle, for example on an indicator.

subtopic: Analogue and digital ADCs
question: In a digital ADC, how are the analogue pressure measurements turned into data for processing?

options.text: A servomotor converts them into voltages
An analogue-to-digital converter
A capsule stack drives the display directly through gearing
A synchro changes them into shaft angles

explanation: The pressure transducers produce analogue signals, which are digitised. The microprocessor then computes the air data and sends it on data buses.

subtopic: Redundancy and failure warning
question: If one ADC fails, how can the instruments on that side be restored?

options.text: By selecting the other ADC to supply them
By switching to the standby instruments on that side
By entering air data manually into the ADC
By resetting the pitot heat

explanation: The two ADC systems can be cross-connected so one ADC supplies both sides. The standby instruments remain as a separate, independent backup.

subtopic: Redundancy and failure warning
question: Can the crew enter air data manually into an ADC if its sensors fail?

options.text: Only on the ground, for testing
No, there is no provision for manual input
Yes, using the standby altimeter's subscale knob
Yes, through the flight management system keyboard

explanation: The ADC has no manual input. Instead, built-in test equipment gives prompt indication of any malfunction so that the crew can change to another source.

subtopic: Redundancy and failure warning
question: How is an ADC failure usually shown to the crew on the affected instruments?

options.text: By a stick shaker activation
By the pointers going to their maximum reading
By the instrument lights going out
By a failure flag on the display

explanation: The ADC's monitoring sets a flag, and the indicator shows it rather than continuing to display misleading data. The crew then selects the other ADC or uses the standby instruments.

subtopic: Built-in test equipment
question: When does the power-up BITE of an ADC run?

options.text: Only after an in-flight failure warning
Only when maintenance staff select a test switch
Whenever power is applied
About once every second throughout operation

explanation: Power-up BITE checks the microprocessor, the memory and the air data functions whenever power is applied. Continuous BITE then takes over during operation.

subtopic: Built-in test equipment
question: How often does continuous BITE check an ADC's inputs and outputs?

options.text: About once every second
Once per flight
About once a minute
Only when the crew request it

explanation: Continuous BITE is an automatic check of every stage of input and output throughout operation, roughly every second. Faults are flagged promptly.

subtopic: Built-in test equipment
question: What is the purpose of maintenance BITE in an ADC?

options.text: To allow pilots to calibrate the ADC in flight
To test the ADC continuously during flight
To check the processor and memory when power is first applied
Ground testing, with current and past faults

explanation: Maintenance BITE is selected with a test or test/history switch on the ground. It shows both current faults and those recorded on earlier flights.

subtopic: Built-in test equipment
question: What three types of BITE are found in an ADC?

options.text: Analogue, digital and hybrid
Power-up, continuous and maintenance
Primary, secondary and standby
Preflight, in-flight and post-flight

explanation: Power-up BITE runs at switch-on, continuous BITE runs about once a second, and maintenance BITE is used by engineers on the ground.

subtopic: Advantages of an air data system
question: How does an air data system reduce instrument and lag errors compared with mechanical instruments?

options.text: It heats the static lines
It averages the readings of all three pitot-static systems
Servomotors replace friction-prone linkages
It uses larger pitot tubes

explanation: Friction in linkages is the major cause of instrument error and limits response, causing lag. Electrically servoed indicators largely overcome both problems.

subtopic: Advantages of an air data system
question: Why can an air data system apply position error correction to several outputs at once?

options.text: Each indicator has its own position error correction card
The static vents are corrected by heaters
One computer works out all the quantities
Position error does not exist in an ADC system

explanation: The position error correction can be worked out once, for example in the Mach channel, and applied in the altitude and airspeed channels too. Shaped cams or software tailor it to the aircraft.

subtopic: Advantages of an air data system
question: Which display formats do electrically servoed air data instruments make possible?

options.text: Digital, moving tape and combined displays
Only three-pointer dials
Only round dials with a single pointer and a counter
Only head-up displays

explanation: Freed from mechanical linkages, designers can choose displays that are easier to read and unambiguous. Moving tapes and digital readouts are now standard.

subtopic: Advantages of an air data system
question: How does an air data system make the installation behind the panel "cleaner"?

options.text: It uses one static vent for all systems
Pipes are needed only for the standby instruments
It places all instruments in the avionics bay
It removes the need for any standby instruments at all

explanation: Electrical signals replace long pressure lines to each instrument. Shorter pitot-static lines also reduce error-producing acoustic effects, and maintenance is easier.

subtopic: Advantages of an air data system
question: Why do shorter pitot-static lines reduce errors?

options.text: They reduce the density error of the ASI
They reduce the effect of temperature on the capsules
They prevent the pitot tube from icing
They reduce acoustic effects in the pipes

explanation: Pressure changes travel down the pipes as waves and are delayed and distorted on the way. Short lines from the probes to the ADC minimise these effects.

subtopic: Advantages of an air data system
question: Why is an ADC described as a central source for other systems?

options.text: It powers the other avionics systems
It feeds air data to many other systems
It controls the pitot and static heaters
It is mounted in the centre of the instrument panel

explanation: The same computed altitude, speed, Mach and temperature data serve the instruments, autopilot, FMS, transponder, warning systems and recorders. Each system does not need its own sensors.
